newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-PALMEIRAS SEETHING OVER FEMALE REFEREE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PALMEIRAS SEETHING OVER FEMALE REFEREE.

text.p: Defending champions Palmeiras were seething at a female referee who disallowed a goal and sent off one of their players during their 1-1 draw with Sao Jose in the Sao Paulo championship at the weekend.

Brazilian players do not hesistate to blame male referees for their own shortcomings and Palmeiras did the same to Canadian Sonia Denoncourt after failing to beat their unrated, newly promoted opponents.
"The refereeing was terrible," moaned Palmeiras playmaker Djalminha, who put Palmeiras in front in the 41st minute.
"I can't see any reason to chose a woman for the opening match of the championship," said Palmeiras director Sebastiao Lapola.

Palmeiras, who scored 102 goals and were unbeaten as they won the competition last year, were angry over a disallowed goal and the sending-off of Brazilian international full-back Cafu for a second bookable offence.
But Denoncourt, 32, was praised by Sao Jose president Lindonice de Brito -- the only female president of a club in the Sao Paulo championship.
"Her presence was very important. Here in Sao Jose, women have overcome prejudice," she said after watching her team force a draw in the second half.

The Sao Paulo federation began using foreign referees for important matches last year in an attempt to torpedo frequent accusations -- usually made by the losing side -- that local referees were subject to influences and pressure behind the scenes.

Despite the controversy, the federation, which has taken a series of measures designed to make the competition more attractive and bring fans back to the stadiums, claimed the opening day was a huge success.

The average attendance was 12,047 and the games featuring leading clubs Palmeiras, Corinthians and Santos all took place in packed stadiums, even though they were played over Brazil's carnival weekend.
Innovations include free sandwiches for fans who buy their tickets in advance, live music before games and American-style cheerleaders.

The federation have continued with their time-out experiment. The coach of one side has the right to call a two-minute break in the 30th minute of the first half and his rival the same right in the second half.
